lessons.title: Lesson 1 — Excuse me, do you understand?
lessons.goal: Greet someone politely and say whether you understand English or German

steps.n: Lesson 1. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
We begin with the word for 'English'. Listen and repeat, starting with the end of the word.
Here is how to say 'do you understand'. Listen and repeat.
The word 'Sie' is the polite 'you'. Germans use it with strangers, shopkeepers and anyone they don't know well. We will use it throughout these lessons.
Now ask 'do you understand English?'. Just put the two together.
Say 'English'.
Here is how to say 'excuse me'. Listen and repeat.
'Entschuldigung' is a very useful word. It means both 'excuse me' and 'sorry'. Use it to get attention or to apologise.
Here is how to say 'no'. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'I understand'. Listen and repeat.
Notice that 'ich', the word for 'I', ends in a soft sound made at the back of the mouth. Don't worry if it is not perfect yet; just copy the speaker.
How do you say 'English'?
Here is the word for 'not'. Listen and repeat.
In German, 'not' comes after the verb. So 'I don't understand' is literally 'I understand not'. Listen.
Ask 'do you understand?'
Here is how to say 'German'. Listen and repeat.
Now ask 'do you understand German?'
Ask her whether she understands English.
Here is how to say 'yes'. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'a little'. Listen and repeat.
How do you ask someone 'do you understand?'
Here is 'I don't understand English'. In German you say literally 'I understand no English'. Listen.
Say 'excuse me'.
Now say 'I understand a little German'. 'German' goes at the end.
How do you say 'no'?
Imagine you are in Munich. Stop a woman politely and ask her if she understands English.

steps.q: She answers like this. Does she understand English?

steps.n: No, she doesn't. Say what she said.
Now she asks whether you understand German. Ask that.
Tell her 'yes, a little'.
Say 'I understand'.
Tell her you don't understand.
How do you say 'German'?
Ask him whether he understands German.
Let's review.
You want to get someone's attention. What do you say?
Ask 'do you understand English?'
Say 'I don't understand'.
Tell him you understand a little German.
Listen to the conversation from the beginning once more. You should understand all of it now.

steps.t: Nein. Ich verstehe kein Englisch. Verstehen Sie Deutsch?

steps.n: Well done. In the next lesson you will learn 'good day', 'please', 'thank you', 'I speak', and to ask how someone is. This is the end of lesson one.

lessons.title: Lesson 2 — How are you? Please and thank you
lessons.goal: Greet people at different times of day, ask how they are, say please and thank you, and say what you speak

steps.n: Lesson 2. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Stop a stranger and ask whether she understands English.
Say 'I understand a little German'.
Here is the everyday greeting, 'good day'. Listen and repeat.
'Guten Tag' is the standard polite greeting from late morning until evening. In Bavaria and Austria you will often hear 'Grüß Gott' instead, but 'Guten Tag' is understood everywhere.
Here is 'good morning'. The first word is the same. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'how are you'. Listen and repeat.
Literally this means 'how goes it to you?'. 'Ihnen' is the polite 'you' again, so this is the form for people you address as 'Sie'.
Ask 'do you understand English?'
Here is how to say 'thank you'. Listen and repeat.
Here is the word for 'good' or 'fine'. You heard it in 'Guten Tag'. On its own it sounds like this.
Now answer 'fine, thanks'.
Say 'I don't understand'.
Here is 'and you?'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'fine, thanks. And you?'
Ask 'do you understand English?'
Here is how to say 'do you speak English'. Listen and repeat.
You already know 'Verstehen Sie' for 'do you understand'. 'Sprechen Sie' asks 'do you speak'. Both are formal and polite.
Say 'I don't understand'.
Here is how to say 'I speak'. Listen and repeat.
Now say 'I don't speak English'. Remember, it is literally 'I speak no English'.
Say 'I speak a little German'.
Say 'good day'.
Here is how to say 'please'. Listen and repeat.
'Bitte' is the most flexible word in German. It means 'please', but also 'you're welcome' after 'danke', 'here you are' when handing something over, and 'pardon?' when you didn't hear.
Here is how to say 'goodbye'. Listen and repeat.
'Auf Wiedersehen' literally means 'until we see each other again'. Among friends you will often just hear 'Tschüss'.
Say 'good morning'.
Here is 'also fine'. Listen and repeat.
Greet someone formally in the afternoon.
Now a short scene. It is morning in Hamburg. Greet your neighbour and ask how she is.

steps.expect: Guten Morgen! Wie geht es Ihnen?

steps.t: Guten Morgen! Wie geht es Ihnen?

steps.q: She answers. Listen. How is she?

steps.n: She is fine, and she asked about you. Say 'also fine'.
Ask her whether she speaks English.
She says no. Tell her you speak a little German.
Thank her and say goodbye.
Let's review.
Say 'good day'.
Ask 'how are you?'
Answer 'fine, thanks, and you?'
Say 'please'.
Here is the conversation once more.

steps.t: Guten Morgen! Wie geht es Ihnen?
Nein, ich spreche kein Englisch. Sprechen Sie Deutsch?
Ja, ein bisschen. Danke. Auf Wiedersehen!

steps.n: In the next lesson you will ask where things are, ask how much something costs, and count from one to ten. This is the end of lesson two.

lessons.title: Lesson 3 — Where is it? How much? One to ten
lessons.goal: Ask where something is, ask how much it costs, and count from one to ten

steps.n: Lesson 3. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Say 'good day' and ask whether he speaks English.
Tell him you speak a little German.
Here is how to ask 'where is'. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'the toilet'. Listen and repeat.
German nouns have three genders. 'Die' is the feminine 'the'. You will also meet 'der' for masculine and 'das' for neuter. Learn the little word together with each noun.
Now ask 'where is the toilet?'
Ask 'do you speak English?'
Here is how to say 'the station'. Listen and repeat.
'Bahnhof' is literally 'rail yard'. It is masculine, so it takes 'der'.
Ask 'where is the station?'
Say 'goodbye'.
Here is 'over there'. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'how much does that cost'. Listen and repeat.
'Wie viel' means 'how much'. You already know 'wie' from 'Wie geht es Ihnen?'. 'Das' here means 'that'.
Ask 'do you speak English?'
Now the numbers. Here is 'one'. Listen and repeat.
'Two'.
'Three'.
'Four'.
'Five'.
Count from one to five.
Say 'goodbye'.
Here is the word for the currency, 'euro'. Listen and repeat.
In German the plural of 'Euro' is still 'Euro'. Say 'three euros'.
Now say 'that costs three euros'.
'Six'.
'Seven'.
'Eight'.
'Nine'.
'Ten'.
Count from six to ten.
Ask 'where is'.
Ask how much that costs, then answer 'that costs eight euros'.
Here is 'thank you very much'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'the toilet'.
Now the scene. You are in a café. Ask the waiter politely where the toilet is.

steps.q: He answers. Where is it?

steps.n: Over there. Thank him, then ask how much that costs.

steps.q: Listen to the price. How much is it?

steps.n: Three euros. Hand him the money and say 'three euros, here you are'.
Let's review.
Ask where the toilet is.
Ask 'how much does that cost?'
Count from one to five.
Count from six to ten.
Here is the conversation once more.
Next time you will order food and drink in a restaurant. This is the end of lesson three.

lessons.title: Lesson 4 — I'd like a beer, please
lessons.goal: Order food and drink in a café or restaurant and ask for the bill

steps.n: Lesson 4. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Ask where the toilet is.
Count from one to five.
Here is 'good evening'. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'I would like'. Listen and repeat.
'Ich möchte' is the polite way to ask for anything. The vowel 'ö' is made by saying 'eh' with your lips rounded. Listen to the speaker again.
Here is 'a beer'. Listen and repeat.
Now say 'I would like a beer, please'.
Ask how much that costs.
Here is 'a water'. Listen and repeat.
And 'a coffee'.

Did you notice? It was 'ein Bier', 'ein Wasser', but 'einen Kaffee'. Coffee is masculine, and when it is the thing you want, 'ein' becomes 'einen'. Don't worry about the grammar for now, just copy the phrase.
Say 'I would like a coffee, please'.
Say 'thank you very much'.
Here is how to say 'what would you like'. Listen and repeat.
'Möchten Sie' is the question form, 'would you like'. 'Was' means 'what'.
Ask how much that costs.
Here is 'to eat something'. Listen and repeat.
Now ask 'would you like to eat something?'
Say 'thank you very much'.
Here is 'something to drink'.
Ask 'would you like something to drink?'
Here is another very common way to say 'I would like'. Listen and repeat.
'Ich hätte gern' means the same as 'ich möchte', literally 'I would gladly have'. Waiters hear it all day. 'Gern' on its own means 'gladly' and is what a waiter says to mean 'certainly'.
Here is 'a soup'. Soup is feminine, so it is 'eine'.
Say 'I would like a soup'.
Say 'good evening'.
Here is how to say 'the bill, please'. Listen and repeat.
In Germany you ask for the bill at the table; it does not come by itself. It is normal to round up and tell the waiter the total you want to pay, including a tip of five to ten percent.
Say 'I would like'.
The waiter says 'that makes nine euros'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I'd like a beer, please'.
Order a coffee politely.
Now the scene. It is evening. Greet the waiter.

steps.q: He asks you something. Listen. What does he want to know?

steps.n: He asked what you would like. Order a beer and a water.

steps.expect: Ich möchte ein Bier, bitte. Und ein Wasser.

steps.t: Ich möchte ein Bier, bitte. Und ein Wasser.

steps.n: He asks if you would like something to eat. Say yes, you would like a soup.

steps.expect: Ja, ich hätte gern eine Suppe.

steps.t: Ja, ich hätte gern eine Suppe.

steps.n: Later, ask for the bill.
Let's review.
Order a beer politely.
Ask 'what would you like?'
Ask him if he would like something to eat.
Ask for the bill.
Here is the conversation once more.

steps.t: Ich möchte ein Bier, bitte. Und ein Wasser.
Ja, ich hätte gern eine Suppe.

steps.n: Next time you will ask for directions and take the train. This is the end of lesson four.

lessons.title: Lesson 5 — Straight ahead, then left
lessons.goal: Ask for and understand directions, and buy a train ticket

steps.n: Lesson 5. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Order a coffee politely.
Count from six to ten.
Here is how to say 'straight ahead'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'left'. Listen and repeat.
And 'right'.
Ask where the station is.
Here is 'then'.
Now say 'straight ahead, then left'.
Ask for the bill.
Here is how to say 'is that far'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'on foot'. Listen and repeat.
The letter that looks like a capital B at the end of 'Fuß' is an 'ess-tsett'. It is simply a sharp 's' sound.
Say 'no, five minutes on foot'.
Ask where the station is.
Here is 'the train'. It is masculine.
And 'the bus', also masculine.
Here is 'to Berlin'. 'Nach' is 'to' for towns and countries. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'when does the train leave'. Listen and repeat.
'Fährt' literally means 'drives' or 'travels'. Germans use it for trains, buses and cars alike. 'Wann' means 'when'.
Now ask 'when does the train to Berlin leave?'

steps.t: Wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin?

steps.expect: Wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin?

steps.t: Wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin?

steps.n: Ask for the bill.
Ask 'when does the bus leave?'
Here is 'at ten o'clock'. 'Uhr' means o'clock. Listen and repeat.
Say 'straight ahead'.
Here is how to say 'a ticket to Berlin, please'. Listen and repeat.
On German trains you buy your ticket before boarding, at a machine or counter. On buses and trams in many cities you must also stamp the ticket in the little box on board, or it is not valid.
Say 'left'.
Say 'right'.
Give directions: 'straight ahead, then left'.
Now the scene. You are in Leipzig. Stop someone and ask where the station is.

steps.q: Listen to the answer. Which way do you go?

steps.n: Straight ahead, then left. Ask if it is far.

steps.q: Listen. How long does it take?

steps.n: Five minutes on foot. Thank her and ask when the train to Berlin leaves.

steps.expect: Danke. Wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin?

steps.t: Danke. Wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin?

steps.n: At the station, buy a ticket to Berlin.
Let's review.
How do you say 'straight ahead'?
Ask 'is that far?'
Ask when the train to Berlin leaves.

steps.expect: Wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin?

steps.t: Wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin?

steps.n: Buy a ticket to Berlin.
Here is the conversation once more.

steps.t: Danke. Wann fährt der Zug nach Berlin?

steps.n: Next time you will tell the time and learn the days of the week. This is the end of lesson five.

lessons.title: Lesson 6 — What time is it? Days of the week
lessons.goal: Ask and tell the time, and talk about today, tomorrow and the days of the week

steps.n: Lesson 6. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Give directions: 'straight ahead, then left'.
Say 'a ticket to Berlin, please'.
Here is how to say 'what time is it'. Listen and repeat.
You know 'wie viel' from 'how much does that cost'. 'Wie viel Uhr ist es' is literally 'how much clock is it'. You may also hear 'Wie spät ist es', 'how late is it'.
Here is 'it is three o'clock'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'it is seven o'clock'.
Ask when the bus leaves.
Two more numbers. 'Eleven'.
'Twelve'.
Say 'it is twelve o'clock'.
Say 'at ten o'clock'.
Here is 'half past three'. Listen carefully.
Careful! 'Halb vier' is literally 'half four', but it means half past THREE, half way to four. This catches out every learner. 'Halb zehn' is half past nine.
So, say 'half past nine'.
Say 'at half past three'.
Ask when the bus leaves.
Here is 'today'. Listen and repeat.
And 'tomorrow'. You already know this word from 'good morning'.
Ask 'and tomorrow?'
Say 'at ten o'clock'.
Now the days of the week. 'Monday'.
'Tuesday'.
'Wednesday'. Literally 'mid-week'.
Say Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday.
Ask 'what time is it?'
'Thursday'.
'Friday'.
'Saturday'.
'Sunday'.
Say Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
Most days end in 'Tag', the word for 'day'. In northern Germany Saturday is often called 'Sonnabend', 'Sunday eve', but 'Samstag' is understood everywhere.
Say 'it is three o'clock'.
Say 'tomorrow is Sunday'.
Say 'today is Friday'.
Ask someone the time.
Here is 'there is no bus tomorrow', literally 'tomorrow drives no bus'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'on Monday'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'the train to Berlin leaves on Monday at eight o'clock'.

steps.t: Der Zug nach Berlin fährt am Montag um acht Uhr.

steps.expect: Der Zug nach Berlin fährt am Montag um acht Uhr.

steps.n: Say 'half past three'.
Say 'at half past three'.
Now the scene. You are at a bus stop in Dresden. Ask a woman politely what time it is.

steps.expect: Entschuldigung, wie viel Uhr ist es?

steps.t: Entschuldigung, wie viel Uhr ist es?

steps.q: Listen. What time is it?

steps.n: Three o'clock. Thank her and ask when the bus leaves.

steps.q: Listen. When does it leave?

steps.n: At half past three. Now ask 'and tomorrow?'
Let's review.
Ask 'what time is it?'
Say 'at half past three'.
Say Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday.
Say Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday.
Here is the conversation once more.

steps.t: Entschuldigung, wie viel Uhr ist es?
Morgen fährt kein Bus. Morgen ist Sonntag.

steps.n: Next time you will introduce yourself and your family. This is the end of lesson six.

lessons.title: Lesson 7 — My name is... This is my wife
lessons.goal: Introduce yourself and your family, and say where you come from

steps.n: Lesson 7. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Say 'tomorrow is Sunday'.
Say 'it is twelve o'clock'.
Here is how to say 'my name is', literally 'I am called'. Listen and repeat.
Now say your own name after it. For example, 'Ich heiße Tom Miller'. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'what is your name'. Listen and repeat.
Germans introduce themselves with first name and surname, and adults who have just met address each other as 'Herr' or 'Frau' plus the surname. A short handshake is normal.
Ask what time it is.
Here is 'pleased to meet you', literally 'it pleases me'. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'where do you come from'. Listen and repeat.
'Woher' means 'where from'. You know 'wo' from 'wo ist'.
Here is how to say 'I come from America'. Listen and repeat.
Ask what time it is.
Here is how to say 'this is my wife'. Listen and repeat.
'Frau' means both 'wife' and 'woman', and it is also the title 'Mrs' or 'Ms'. 'Meine' is 'my' for feminine nouns.
Here is 'my husband'. 'Mann' is masculine, so it is 'mein' without the e.
Say 'this is my husband'.
Say 'today'.
Here is how to say 'do you have children'. Listen and repeat.
'Haben Sie' means 'do you have'. You will use it a lot: 'Haben Sie Zeit?', 'Haben Sie ein Zimmer?'.
Say 'my name is'.
Here is 'a son'. Listen and repeat.
And 'a daughter'.
Now answer 'yes, a son and a daughter'.

steps.t: Ja, einen Sohn und eine Tochter.

steps.expect: Ja, einen Sohn und eine Tochter.

steps.t: Ja, einen Sohn und eine Tochter.

steps.n: Say 'today'.
Here is 'I have'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I have a daughter'.
Say 'my name is'.
Ask 'what is your name?'
Now the scene. You arrive at the hotel. The owner greets you and gives her name. Listen.

steps.t: Guten Tag, ich heiße Anna Weber. Wie heißen Sie?

steps.n: Give your name as Tom Miller and say 'pleased to meet you'.

steps.expect: Ich heiße Tom Miller. Freut mich.

steps.t: Ich heiße Tom Miller. Freut mich.

steps.q: She asks you something. Listen. What does she want to know?

steps.n: Where you come from. Say you come from America, and introduce your wife, Sarah.

steps.expect: Ich komme aus Amerika. Das ist meine Frau, Sarah.

steps.t: Ich komme aus Amerika. Das ist meine Frau, Sarah.

steps.n: She asks if you have children. Say 'yes, a son and a daughter'.

steps.expect: Ja, einen Sohn und eine Tochter.

steps.t: Ja, einen Sohn und eine Tochter.

steps.n: Let's review.
Ask him his name.
Ask 'where do you come from?'
Say 'this is my wife'.
Ask 'do you have children?'
Here is the conversation once more.

steps.t: Guten Tag, ich heiße Anna Weber. Wie heißen Sie?
Ich heiße Tom Miller. Freut mich.
Ich komme aus Amerika. Das ist meine Frau, Sarah.
Freut mich sehr. Haben Sie Kinder?
Ja, einen Sohn und eine Tochter.

steps.n: Next time you will say what you like and what you prefer. This is the end of lesson seven.

lessons.title: Lesson 8 — I like wine, I prefer beer
lessons.goal: Say what you like and don't like, what you prefer, and offer someone a drink

steps.n: Lesson 8. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Ask 'would you like something to drink?'
Introduce your wife.
Here is 'yes, gladly'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'wine'. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'I like drinking wine'. Listen and repeat.
This is the most common way to say you like doing something: the verb, then 'gern'. 'Ich trinke gern' is literally 'I drink gladly'.
Ask whether he has children.
Say 'I like drinking beer'.
Here is 'red wine'. Listen and repeat.
And 'white wine'.
Here is 'or'.
Ask 'red wine or white wine?'
Say 'I come from America'.
Here is how to say 'do you like wine'. Listen and repeat.
'Mögen' is 'to like' for things and people. For activities Germans prefer the 'gern' construction you just learned.
Ask whether he has children.
Here is 'I like'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'I don't like wine'. Because 'Wein' is masculine, 'no' becomes 'keinen'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I come from America'.
Here is how to say 'I prefer to drink beer'. Listen and repeat.
'Lieber' means 'rather' or 'preferably'. 'Gern' is 'gladly', 'lieber' is 'more gladly'. Swap one for the other and you have expressed a preference.
Someone offers you a drink. Accept: 'yes, gladly'.
Here is how to say 'what do you like to eat'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'bread and cheese'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I like eating bread and cheese'.

steps.t: Ich esse gern Brot und Käse.

steps.expect: Ich esse gern Brot und Käse.

steps.t: Ich esse gern Brot und Käse.

steps.n: Someone offers you a drink. Accept: 'yes, gladly'.
When Germans raise their glasses they say 'Prost' and look each other in the eye. Say it.
Say 'I like drinking wine'.
Ask 'red wine or white wine?'
Now the scene. You are visiting a German friend. She asks if you would like something to drink. Accept and say you like drinking wine.

steps.expect: Ja, gern. Ich trinke gern Wein.

steps.t: Ja, gern. Ich trinke gern Wein.

steps.q: She asks you a question. Listen.

steps.n: Red or white. Say 'red wine, please', then ask if she likes wine.

steps.q: Listen to her answer. Does she like wine?

steps.t: Nein, ich mag keinen Wein. Ich trinke lieber Bier.

steps.n: No, she prefers beer. She asks what you like to eat. Tell her you like bread and cheese.

steps.expect: Ich esse gern Brot und Käse.

steps.t: Ich esse gern Brot und Käse.

steps.n: Let's review.
Say that you like to drink wine.
Ask 'do you like wine?'
Say 'I prefer to drink beer'.
Ask 'what do you like to eat?'
Here is the conversation once more.

steps.t: Ja, gern. Ich trinke gern Wein.
Nein, ich mag keinen Wein. Ich trinke lieber Bier.
Ich esse gern Brot und Käse.

steps.n: Next time you will talk about yesterday, and what you did. This is the end of lesson eight.

lessons.title: Lesson 9 — Where were you yesterday?
lessons.goal: Talk about the past: where you were and what you did, ate and drank

steps.n: Lesson 9. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Say 'I prefer to drink beer'.
Ask what his name is.
Here is 'yesterday'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'I was'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'in Berlin'.
Say 'I was in Berlin'.
Ask what he likes to eat.
Say 'yesterday I was in Berlin'. Start with 'yesterday', then the verb comes straight after.
Did you notice? 'Gestern war ich', not 'gestern ich war'. In German the verb is always the second idea in the sentence.
Here is how to say 'where were you'. Listen and repeat.
Ask 'where were you yesterday?'
Say 'I don't like wine'.
Here is 'it was very good'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'nice' or 'beautiful'. You know it from 'danke schön'.
Here is how to say 'what did you do'. Listen and repeat.
Spoken German talks about the past with 'haben' plus a form that usually begins with 'ge' and goes to the end of the sentence. 'Gemacht' is 'done'. Literally: 'what have you done?'
Ask what he likes to eat.
Here is 'eaten'. Listen and repeat.
Now say 'I ate well', literally 'I have well eaten'.
Say 'I don't like wine'.
Here is 'drunk'.
Ask 'what did you drink?'
Say 'I drank a beer'.
Say 'yesterday'.
Here is 'seen'.
And 'a lot', 'much'.
Say 'I saw a lot'.
Here is 'of course'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'I was'.
Say 'I was in Berlin'.
Now the scene. It is Monday. Your colleague asks where you were yesterday. Listen.
Tell her you were in Berlin.

steps.q: She asks a question. Listen. What does she want to know?

steps.n: What you did. Say you saw a lot, and you ate well.

steps.expect: Ich habe viel gesehen. Und ich habe gut gegessen.

steps.t: Ich habe viel gesehen. Und ich habe gut gegessen.

steps.n: She asks what you drank. Say 'a beer, of course. It was very good.'

steps.expect: Ein Bier, natürlich. Es war sehr gut.

steps.t: Ein Bier, natürlich. Es war sehr gut.

steps.n: Let's review.
Ask where she was yesterday.
Ask 'what did you do?'
Say 'I ate well'.
Say 'I saw a lot'.
Here is the conversation once more.

steps.t: Ich habe viel gesehen. Und ich habe gut gegessen.
Ein Bier, natürlich. Es war sehr gut.

steps.n: Next time you will make plans to meet someone. This is the end of lesson nine.

lessons.title: Lesson 10 — Do you have time tomorrow evening?
lessons.goal: Make plans: ask if someone has time, suggest going out together, and agree on when and where to meet

steps.n: Lesson 10. Let's go! Listen, then say it with me.
Ask where she was yesterday.
Say 'I like drinking wine'.
Here is the word for 'time'. Listen and repeat.
Here is how to say 'do you have time'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'tomorrow evening'. You know both words.
Now ask 'do you have time tomorrow evening?'. The time goes in the middle.
Ask 'what did you do?'
Here is 'I have time'. Listen and repeat.
Now 'tomorrow evening I have time'. Remember, the verb stays in second place, so it is 'morgen Abend habe ich Zeit'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'why?'.
Say 'I drank a beer'.
Here is 'to go out to eat', literally 'eat go'. Listen and repeat.
Here is 'shall we', literally 'want we'. Listen and repeat.
'Wir' means 'we'. 'Wollen wir' is the easiest way to suggest doing something together.
Now ask 'shall we go out to eat?'
Ask 'what did you do?'
Here is 'together'. Listen and repeat.
Ask 'shall we go out to eat together?'
Here is how to say 'at what time'. Listen and repeat.
Answer 'at seven'.
Say 'I drank a beer'.
Here is how to say 'let's meet at the station'. Listen and repeat.
Germans take punctuality seriously. If you agree on seven, arrive at seven, or a few minutes early. Being late without a message is considered rude.
Say 'let's meet at seven'.
Ask 'do you have time?'
Here is 'see you tomorrow', literally 'until tomorrow'. Listen and repeat.
Say 'tomorrow evening'.
Ask if she has time tomorrow evening.
Now the scene. Ask your colleague whether he has time tomorrow evening.

steps.q: Listen to his answer. Does he have time?

steps.t: Ja, morgen Abend habe ich Zeit. Warum?

steps.n: Yes, he does, and he asks why. Suggest going out to eat together.

steps.q: He agrees and asks something. Listen.

steps.n: At what time. Say 'at seven? Let's meet at the station.'

steps.expect: Um sieben? Treffen wir uns am Bahnhof.

steps.t: Um sieben? Treffen wir uns am Bahnhof.

steps.n: He agrees. Say 'good, see you tomorrow!'
Let's review.
Ask him if he has time.
Suggest going out to eat.
Ask 'at what time?'
Say 'let's meet at the station'.
Here is the conversation once more.

steps.n: Congratulations. You have finished the course. You can now greet people, order, shop, ask directions, tell the time, introduce your family and make plans in German. Keep listening, keep speaking, and remember: 'Wie bitte? Langsamer, bitte.' will always get you another chance. Auf Wiedersehen!
